entry: Top-flight men's national [[Association football|football]] tournament of [[South America]], held every four years. Known as the South American Football Championship until 1975, it is the oldest extant continental football competition. Uruguay won the first edition, in 1916. Eight of the ten CONMEBOL national teams have won the title, with Ecuador and Venezuela yet to win. [[Argentina]] has won the most titles, 16, and has hosted the tournament nine times. Since 1993 the field has generally included 12 teams: all 10 CONMEBOL teams and two from other confederations. The 2016 and 2024 editions had 16 teams. The United States hosted in 2016 and 2024.

Annual South American club [[Association football|football]] competition, the highest level of club competition on the continent. Organized by CONMEBOL since 1960, it is named after the Libertadores, the leaders of the [[Spanish American wars of independence]] and Brazilian independence. [[Argentina|Argentina's]] Independiente has won it seven times, the most of any club. Argentine and [[Brazil|Brazilian]] clubs have 25 wins each. Brazilian clubs hold a record winning streak of seven titles in a row, starting in 2019.

Capital and most populous city of [[Denmark]], mainly on the island of Zealand. Settled as a Viking fishing village in the 10th century, it became the Danish capital in the early 15th century, with an urban population of 1.4 million. The city flourished as the cultural and economic center of [[Scandinavia]] during the [[Renaissance]]. In 1807 a British fleet bombarded it during the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. After [[World War II]], the Finger Plan guided housing and business development along five urban railway routes. Copenhagen is the cultural, economic and governmental center of Denmark and one of the major financial centers of Northern Europe. Its economy has grown rapidly in [[Information technology|information technology]], pharmaceuticals and clean technology. The Øresund Bridge links it with Malmö in [[Sweden]]. The University of Copenhagen, founded in 1479, is the oldest university in Denmark.

Inorganic compound, CuSO₄, most common as the bright blue pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O. Its anhydrous form is white. Older names for the pentahydrate include blue vitriol and bluestone. Industrially it is made by treating [[Copper|copper]] metal with hot concentrated [[Sulfuric acid]]. It is toxic if ingested. In high school and general chemistry it is used as an electrolyte for galvanic cells.

Species of [[Fungus|fungus]], also called the shaggy ink cap, lawyer's wig or shaggy mane. Its young caps are white and covered in scales. When young it is an excellent edible mushroom, but it spoils quickly. Its gills turn black and dissolve into an inky liquid within hours of being picked or depositing spores. It often grows on lawns, gravel roads and waste areas in the Northern Hemisphere. It appears to have been introduced to Australia, New Zealand and Iceland.

[[Oriental Orthodox Churches|Oriental Orthodox]] Christian church based in [[Egypt]], also known as the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria. Its head is the pope of Alexandria, who presides from Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral in [[Cairo]]. Tradition holds that Saint Mark the Evangelist founded the church in the middle of the 1st century AD. Its liturgy uses the Bohairic dialect of Coptic, and its service books have [[Arabic]] text in parallel columns. The see moved from [[Alexandria]] to Cairo in the 12th century. Disputes over the nature of Christ put the Oriental Orthodox churches in schism after the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451.

[[Christianity|Christian]] ethnoreligious group native to [[Egypt]], descended from the [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]]. Most belong to the [[Coptic Orthodox Church]], with a minority in the Coptic Catholic Church. Copts are the largest Christian population in Egypt and the [[Middle East]], and make up roughly 5 to 15 percent of Egypt's population. Their traditional language, Coptic, is a direct descendant of Demotic Egyptian. Copts have faced cycles of persecution and relative tolerance. Most live in Upper Egypt, where they often work in blue-collar jobs; those in Cairo and Alexandria have relatively high educational attainment.

Form of [[Intellectual property|intellectual property]] giving exclusive rights to copy, distribute, adapt and perform a creative work for a limited time. Copyright protects the original expression of an idea, not the idea itself. Its limits include fair use in the United States and fair dealing in the [[United Kingdom]]. Rights normally include reproduction, control over derivative works, distribution, public performance and moral rights such as attribution. Copyright usually expires 50 to 100 years after the creator dies, depending on jurisdiction, and the work then enters the [[Public domain|public domain]]. The concept developed after the [[Printing press|printing press]] came into use in Europe. The Statute of Anne of 1710 was the first legislation to protect copyrights in England and Scotland. The Berne International Copyright Convention of 1886 gave protection among signatory countries, but the United States did not join until 1989.

Colonial marine invertebrate of the subphylum Anthozoa, in the phylum [[Cnidaria]]. A coral colony consists of many genetically identical polyps, each a sac-like animal with tentacles around a central mouth. Each polyp secretes a [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]] exoskeleton, and over many generations a colony can form a skeleton several meters across. Colonies grow by asexual reproduction, and corals also spawn sexually, often around a full moon. Most corals obtain most of their energy from [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] by symbiotic [[Dinoflagellate|dinoflagellates]] called zooxanthellae, which give them their color. Cold-water corals such as *Lophelia* survive at depths of up to 3,300 meters. Until the 18th century corals were thought to be plants, but [[William Herschel]] used a microscope to show that they have the thin cell membranes of animals.

Marginal sea of the South Pacific off the northeast coast of [[Australia]]. It contains numerous islands and reefs, and includes the [[Great Barrier Reef]], which UNESCO declared a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1981. The Battle of the Coral Sea, a major confrontation of [[World War II]], was fought in May 1942 between the navies of the [[Empire of Japan]] and the United States and Australia. The battle thwarted Japanese plans to invade [[Port Moresby]] in New Guinea. Much of the sea is protected, including by the French Natural Park of the Coral Sea and the Australian Coral Sea Marine Park. Its warm climate brings frequent rains and [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]], and its reefs and islands are a popular tourist destination.

Underwater ecosystem formed from colonies of reef-building [[Coral|corals]] held together by [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]]. Coral reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. Shallow reefs occupy less than 0.1% of the world's ocean area but provide a home for at least 25% of marine species. Most reefs grow best in warm, shallow, clear and agitated water. Most coral reefs formed after the [[Last Glacial Period]], when melting ice raised sea levels and flooded continental shelves. [[Charles Darwin]] proposed that a fringing reef around a subsiding volcanic island becomes a barrier reef and finally an [[Atoll|atoll]]. Shallow tropical reefs have declined by 50% since 1950, threatened by excess nutrients, rising ocean heat, acidification, overfishing and pollution.

Marine fish found among or closely associated with [[Coral reef|coral reefs]]. Coral reefs occupy less than 1% of the surface area of the world's oceans but provide a home for 25% of marine fish species. The Indo-Pacific has an estimated 4,000–5,000 reef fish species, and the greater Caribbean has another 500–700. Most are ray-finned fishes, and many have spines that lock in place or are venomous. Some use [[Camouflage|cryptic coloration]] to avoid predators, while small fish hide in crevices or shoal. Surgeonfishes are [[Herbivore|herbivores]] that graze turf algae and also clean marine turtles. Habitat loss, pollution and overfishing threaten reef fish.

Large group of elapid snakes, divided into Old World and New World coral snakes. The 83 New World species, in the genera *Micruroides* and *Micrurus*, range from the [[Southern United States|southern United States]] to [[Argentina]]. The 27 Old World species live in Asia and Africa. Most are secretive, burrowing snakes that spend much of their time beneath the ground or in leaf litter, and they feed mainly on smaller snakes and lizards. Their neurotoxic venom acts slowly, and bites are seldom lethal. As of 2018, only two confirmed fatalities had been documented in the [[United States]] in the preceding 100 years from the genus *Micrurus*. Coral snakes account for less than one percent of snake bites each year in the United States.

Filipino politician, 11th president of the [[Philippines]] (1986–1992). The first woman to hold the office, she led the 1986 People Power Revolution, a nonviolent movement that ended the two-decade rule of [[Ferdinand Marcos]] and led to the establishment of the democratic Fifth Philippine Republic. Her husband, opposition leader Benigno Aquino Jr., was assassinated in 1983. As president she oversaw the [[Constitution|1987 Constitution]], which limited presidential power and re-established a bicameral Congress. Her administration pursued peace talks that led to the creation of the [[Mindanao|Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao]]. It faced several coup attempts and the 1987 Mendiola Massacre, in which security forces killed protesters.

Genus of ascomycete fungi, most of them endoparasites of [[Insect|insects]] and other [[Arthropod|arthropods]]. Variants of cordyceps have been used in Chinese medicine for more than 1,500 years. The fungus grows through its host as mycelium, replacing the host's tissue. In *Ophiocordyceps unilateralis*, infected ants are manipulated to climb vegetation and bite leaves before they die, a process known as summit disease. *Cordyceps militaris* is cultivated commercially for compounds such as cordycepin.

Greek island in the [[Ionian Sea]], one of the Ionian Islands in western Greece. The island is marked by numerous battles and conquests. Ancient Korkyra took part in the Battle of Sybota, a catalyst for the [[Peloponnesian War]]. From 1204 Corfu was part of the [[Republic of Venice]], which repulsed several [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] sieges, and it became one of the most fortified places in Europe. The British ruled from 1815, after the [[Napoleonic Wars]], until the island was ceded to Greece in 1864. Its old town was added to the [[UNESCO]] World Heritage List in 2007.

Annual herb of the [[Apiaceae]] family, native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its leaves, known as cilantro in the U.S., have a fresh, slightly [[Citrus|citrus]] taste for most people. Due to variations in the gene OR6A2, some people perceive the flavor as soapy or rotten. The fresh leaves and dried seeds are both used in cooking, and the plant is included in Peruvian, Mexican, Indian and Southeast Asian cuisines. It has been cultivated for more than 3,000 years, with evidence from [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] tombs.

Pseudo-force acting on moving objects within a rotating frame of reference. Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis described it in an 1835 paper on the energy yield of machines with rotating parts, such as waterwheels. On Earth the force deflects moving air and water to the right of their direction in the [[Northern Hemisphere|Northern Hemisphere]] and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. This shapes large-scale winds and ocean currents and causes the rotation of [[Cyclone|cyclones]]. The effect is greatest near the poles and vanishes at the [[Equator]]. It is imperceptible for everyday objects but matters for large-scale atmospheric motion and for [[Artillery|artillery]] and missile trajectories.

Second-largest city in the [[Republic of Ireland]], in the province of Munster. The city center is an island between two channels of the River Lee, which lead to Cork Harbour, one of the world's largest natural harbors. Founded as a monastic settlement in the 6th century, Cork was expanded by Viking settlers around 915. Its charter was granted by Prince John in 1185. The city is nicknamed the rebel city for its support for the Yorkist cause in the [[Wars of the Roses]]. It had a population of 224,004 at the 2022 census.

American author of [[Western (genre)|Western]], post-apocalyptic and Southern Gothic fiction. He wrote twelve novels, two plays and five screenplays, in a sparse style with little punctuation and attribution. His works often include graphic violence. *Blood Meridian* (1985) is now regarded as his magnum opus. *All the Pretty Horses* won the National Book Award in 1992, and *The Road* won the 2007 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. The 2007 film adaptation of *No Country for Old Men* won four [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], including Best Picture.

Family of about 40 species of fish-eating aquatic birds, known as cormorants and shags. Cormorants are medium-to-large birds with webbed feet, long hooked bills and mostly dark [[Feather|feathers]]. They dive from the surface to catch fish, propelling themselves underwater with their feet and wings, and some species dive as deep as 45 meters. Their relatively short wings are suited to underwater movement, which makes flight costly. Colonies nest on seacoasts, in trees, on islets or on cliffs, and some species have colonized inland waters. The family is found in all areas of the world except the central Pacific islands.

American business magnate in railroads and shipping, nicknamed the Commodore. After working in his father's business, he rose to leadership in inland and coastal shipping, then invested in the railroad industry, which transformed the geography of the United States. He was one of the richest Americans in history and the patriarch of the [[Vanderbilt family|Vanderbilt family]]. He provided the initial gift to found Vanderbilt University in [[Nashville, Tennessee]]. For his monopolies in shipping and railroads, facilitated in part by political manipulation, he is often described as either a captain of industry or a robber baron.

Private [[Ivy League]] research university in Ithaca, [[New York (state)|New York]]. Co-founded in 1865 by Ezra Cornell and Andrew Dickson White as a nonsectarian, co-educational institution. As of fall 2024 it had 16,128 undergraduate and 10,665 postgraduate students. It is one of three private land-grant universities in the United States. Satellite campuses include two in [[New York City]] and a medical school branch in Al Rayyan, [[Qatar]].

Genus of about 30–60 species of woody plants in the family Cornaceae, known as dogwoods. Most species are deciduous [[Tree|trees]] or [[Shrub|shrubs]], though some are evergreen and a few are nearly herbaceous subshrubs. Several species have small flower heads surrounded by large, typically white, petal-like bracts. The genus is native throughout much of temperate and boreal Eurasia and [[North America]], with [[China]], [[Japan]] and the southeastern [[United States]] especially rich in native species. Notable species include *Cornus florida*, the widely cultivated flowering dogwood of eastern North America, and *Cornus kousa*, the Kousa dogwood of eastern Asia.

Ceremonial county in South West England, one of the Celtic nations and the homeland of the Cornish people. It is the westernmost part of the South West Peninsula and the southernmost county in the United Kingdom. It is bordered by the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the north and west, [[Devon]] to the east and the [[English Channel]] to the south. The county is predominantly rural. In the 7th century the Britons of Cornwall came into conflict with the [[Wessex|Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Wessex]], and the boundary was set at the Tamar by King [[Æthelstan]] in 936.
